ops.text: Vendor shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless Customer and its Affiliates from and against any third-party claim, and all resulting damages, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees), to the extent arising out of (a) an allegation that the Services or Deliverables infringe or misappropriate any intellectual property right; (b) Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; (c) any unauthorized access to, or disclosure of, Customer Data caused by Vendor; or (d) Vendor's gross negligence or wilful misconduct. Customer shall give Vendor written notice of the claim, Vendor shall control its defence and settlement, and Customer shall provide reasonable cooperation. Customer's indemnification obligations under this Agreement are limited to third-party claims arising from Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of Applicable Law.

quote: 9.3 Customer may terminate an Order Form immediately if Vendor suffers a material Security Incident, repeatedly misses a critical service level, violates Applicable Law in performing the Services, or infringes a third party's intellectual property and cannot provide the remedies required by Section 20.5.
rationale: There is no indemnification clause anywhere in the Agreement: the numbering jumps from Section 19 (Warranties) to Section 21 (Limitation of Liability), and searches for "indemnify", "hold harmless", "defend", and infringement remedies return no operative grant. Sections 9.3 ("remedies required by Section 20.5"), 19.4, 19.5, 21.3, 29.2, and 30.5 all presuppose indemnification obligations and indemnified parties that the document never creates, so Customer has no Vendor IP or misconduct indemnity — walk-away territory. We insert a new Section 20.1 at the preferred level (Vendor defence/indemnity for Services and Deliverables IP infringement, Vendor's breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused unauthorized access to Customer Data, and gross negligence/wilful misconduct, with notice, control of defence, and cooperation) and cap any Customer indemnity at Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of law. We deliberately did not take the fallback: its 3× annual fees super-cap would be worse for us than Section 21.3, which already treats indemnification obligations as uncapped Excluded Claims.

verification.notes: Position-complete at the preferred level: all ten preferred elements are delivered in one inserted paragraph (defend/indemnify/hold harmless for Customer and Affiliates; IP, breach of Applicable Law, Vendor-caused Customer Data incident, and gross negligence/wilful misconduct limbs; notice, Vendor control of defence and settlement, reasonable cooperation; and an express cap on Customer's indemnity to Customer-provided content and Customer's breach of Applicable Law). Fallback is incomplete (no procure/modify/replace ladder, no refund fallback, no 3x annual Fees super-cap), but that is immaterial because the preferred level is fully met. The drafter's reasoning for skipping the super-cap is sound: Section 21.3 already lists indemnification obligations as uncapped Excluded Claims, so importing a 3x cap would be a downgrade. Minimal: the insertion tracks the model language for a missing clause, adds no survival tail, no at-own-expense wording, no extra damages categories or procedures beyond the notice/control/cooperation mechanics the checklist requires, and no retained language was deleted or paraphrased. Intent preserved: Section 9.3's termination trigger, Section 19.5's anti-disclaimer sentence, and Section 21.3's Excluded Claims all reference indemnification and now have an operative obligation to attach to; nothing in the insertion contradicts retained allocation, timing, or payment mechanics. Two drafting hygiene points to verify before sending (neither defeats completeness): (i) confirm "Affiliates" is a defined term in the Agreement — it is not among the resolved definitions supplied; if it is undefined, use "its affiliates" in lower case or add the definition. (ii) Section 9.3 still cross-refers to "the remedies required by Section 20.5"; numbering the insertion as Section 20.1 leaves that pointer dangling. This defect pre-existed the redline and curing it with a procure/modify/replace ladder would exceed the preferred checklist, so either renumber the insertion so the cross-reference resolves or flag the stale reference to Vendor as a conforming-change item.

quote: 14.2 Vendor exclusively owns every Deliverable created for Customer. Customer receives a revocable, non-transferable licence to use a Deliverable only during the applicable Order Form term.
rationale: Section 14.2 gives Vendor exclusive ownership of every Deliverable created for (and paid for by) Customer and leaves Customer only a revocable, non-transferable licence limited to the Order Form term. That fails even the fallback, which requires a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense Deliverables. The rest of the IP architecture already sits at our preferred position: Customer owns Customer Data with Vendor's rights limited to processing it to provide, secure, support and improve the Services (14.1); Vendor retains Vendor Technology, defined as its pre-existing technology (14.3, 1.8); Customer has a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to Vendor Technology embedded in a Deliverable (13.2, 14.3); and no joint ownership arises absent a signed instrument setting out exploitation rights (14.4). The shortest complete cure is therefore to reverse 14.2 to Customer ownership with an express assignment, which leaves 13.2, 14.3 and 10.1 intact.

verification.notes: The single operation rewrites only Section 14.2, the one clause that failed the playbook (Vendor exclusive ownership with a revocable, term-limited, non-transferable licence back). Deleting the old second sentence was necessary, not cosmetic: a revocable Order-Form-term licence to Customer would directly contradict the new Customer ownership. Preferred level is complete on the operative text: ownership plus present assignment (14.2 as revised), Vendor retains pre-existing IP (14.3 with 1.8), perpetual/irrevocable/royalty-free (and worldwide, fully paid) licence to embedded Vendor Technology (13.2, cross-referenced by 14.3), Customer Data ownership with Vendor limited to service-delivery processing (14.1), and no default joint ownership (14.4). No new Vendor rights were created: nothing assigns Customer IP or Customer Data to Vendor, and the Vendor Data right remains "solely to provide, secure, support, and improve the Services for Customer," which is service delivery rather than independent exploitation. Intent is preserved: the 14.3 cross-reference to "the perpetual licence in Section 13.2" still resolves, the Vendor Technology identification and third-party-material approval protections survive, and the feedback mechanics in 14.4 are untouched. No dangling defined term or orphan cross-reference results. No extras were added — no survival tail, indemnity, escrow, moral-rights waiver, further-assurances covenant, or expense allocation — so the redline stays inside the IP checklist. Optional polish only (do not treat as a defect): the drafter could add "and all work product" after "Deliverable" in 14.2 for clarity, but the 1.4 definition already sweeps in Order-Form-identified work product, so the current wording is sufficient.

quote: 21.1 Except for Excluded Claims, each Party's total aggregate liability arising out of or relating to this Agreement shall not exceed the greater of the Fees paid or payable by Customer during the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. The cap is mutual and applies regardless of the form of action or number of claims.
rationale: The clause meets the preferred position in full. § 21.1 imposes an expressly mutual aggregate cap at the greater of Fees paid or payable in the twelve months preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000. § 21.2 excludes indirect, incidental, special, exemplary, punitive and consequential damages mutually ("neither Party"), and helpfully confirms that Customer Data restoration, replacement services, notice and incident-response costs are direct damages. § 21.3 places outside the cap each Party's breach of confidentiality, data-protection or security obligations, indemnification obligations, gross negligence, wilful misconduct or fraud, and infringement or misappropriation of the other Party's IP, and confirms Customer's payment obligation is not damages subject to the Section. "Fees" (§ 1.5) is a substantive recurring subscription/professional services/usage fee base, so the cap is not illusory; § 21.4 preserves each cap independently and prevents the exclusions from swallowing unlawfully limited liability. Two immaterial points noted only for the record: Fees exclude a one-time implementation charge unless an Order Form says otherwise, and the payment carve-out is confined to "undisputed Fees for conforming Services" (a narrowing in our favour). No redline required.

quote: Vendor acknowledges that Customer has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment.
rationale: Section 12.3 (p0044) expressly preserves our freedom to develop, acquire, license, sell or use any product or service and to engage any supplier, and records that Customer has made no exclusivity commitment. No clause anywhere imposes a sole-supplier, all-requirements, or no-third-party-procurement obligation on us, so the rule sits at the preferred position. Section 7.2 (p0026) is a disclose-and-match / most-favoured-offer mechanic and does not prohibit engaging another provider once honoured, so it is handled under MFN, not exclusivity. Section 2.1 (p0012) is a take-or-pay minimum-volume commitment (and Section 12.4's competing-product covenant a non-compete); those are minimum-commitment and restrictive-covenant issues for their own rules and are not sourcing exclusivity, so we do not flag them twice here.

rationale: Section 12.4 binds Customer with an undefined-scope non-compete ("any product or service that competes with Vendor"), covering development, marketing, sale and acquisition, in any territory, for the term plus 24 months. That is walk-away territory on two counts: a post-term restraint longer than 12 months and undefined scope; it also fails every fallback element (no named product, post-term application, no internal-development or acquisition carve-out). It further contradicts Section 12.3, in which Vendor acknowledges Customer "has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment." We therefore reverse the prohibition to the preferred position so Customer carries no non-compete or field-of-use restriction, leaving Section 12.3 consistent.

verification.notes: Preferred checklist is complete: the sole element is met in operative language, not merely promised in the margin comment — the prohibition, its 24-month post-term tail, and the "in any territory" field/territory reach are all eliminated from Section 12.4. The edit is confined to the offending sentence in 12.4. It adds no survival tail, no expense allocation, no procedure, and no requirement outside the NONCOMPETE checklist, and it leaves Section 12.3 (favourable to Customer) untouched. Reversing 12.4 into a permission rather than deleting the paragraph keeps the numbering intact and avoids dangling cross-references; note that the permission largely restates 12.3's existing "Nothing restricts Customer from developing, acquiring, licensing, selling, or using any product or service... in any field or territory," so a straight deletion of 12.4 would be equally acceptable and marginally cleaner if the counterparty objects to the restatement. Minimality holds: the proposal is a single concise insertion in the termination section with no deletions or paraphrase of surrounding text; it adds no survival tail, at-own-expense wording, cost allocation, or procedure beyond the checklist. Extending the trigger to "or any Order Form" is justified by the document's Order Form structure and Section 10.1's reference to "terminated subscription Services" (partial termination), so it is not surplus. Intent is preserved: refund and Deliverables mechanics in 10.2, the access wind-down in 10.1, and the confidentiality return/destroy regime in 16.5 all survive without contradiction; the new clause supplies the substantive Customer Data exit mechanic that was absent. Two housekeeping points for the drafter (not defects in the checklist): (i) the rendered insertion carries no section number although the rationale calls it Section 10.3 — number it so cross-references remain clean; (ii) Section 16.5's retained sentence "Customer Data remains governed by Sections 11 and 15" could be read as excluding the new Section 10 mechanic, and Section 11 is empty, so consider siting the clause in Section 15 or conforming the Section 16.5 cross-reference rather than adding a broad notwithstanding override.

quote: 19.2 For ninety days after delivery or acceptance, whichever is later, each Deliverable will materially conform to its documentation and acceptance criteria. Hosted Services will conform throughout the subscription term.
rationale: Section 19 satisfies the checklist at or above the preferred level. 19.1 warrants Services will be performed in a professional and workmanlike manner and that Services and Deliverables will materially conform to their documentation; 19.2 gives Deliverables a 90-day conformance period and warrants the hosted software (within the defined "Services", § 1.7) will conform throughout the subscription term, which equals or exceeds the 12-month software / 90-day services parameters; 19.3 adds Applicable Law compliance and a no-malicious-code warranty; and 19.4 provides re-performance, repair or replacement plus a refund of Fees paid, expressly non-exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims. 19.5 confirms no disclaimer limits an express warranty, so the disclaimer does not swallow the warranty. Minor points noted only: the malicious-code warranty is qualified to code "intentionally introduced by Vendor", and the Deliverable conformance period is 90 days rather than a flat 12 months; neither is material given the full-term hosted conformance warranty and the acceptance-cycle refund right in 6.2. No redline needed.
